title: Not, in Four Disguises
theme: The negating prefix in- and its assimilated forms il-, im-, ir-
objectives: I can explain why the prefix meaning 'not' is spelled in-, il-, im-, or ir-, using the first letter of the base word.
I can use the base word to work out the meaning of ten words that begin with a negating prefix.
I can choose the right word to describe a plan, an argument, a piece of writing, or a person's behavior.
I can spell the four forms of the prefix correctly in my own writing.
rationale: One prefix wearing four spellings is a real pattern in English, and ten adjectives let students see the single meaning 'not' behind each disguise. The words are grouped by what they describe (plans and tools, writing and reasoning, worth and growth, behavior), so students practice both the word-part rule and precise vocabulary for judging things. The unit shifts students from memorizing words to predicting them: if the base is known, the meaning and the spelling follow. The pattern transfers to dozens of later words such as illegal, impossible, and irregular.

words.def: Not enough, or not good enough, for what is needed.
words.ex: The thin blanket was inadequate for a night in the mountains.
words.ex2: Our old gym was inadequate for the crowd that came to the tournament.
words.nonExample: A jacket that keeps you warm in a blizzard is not inadequate.

morph.note: The prefix keeps its in- spelling before the letter a.

words.rel: when something does not fit or work

apps.academic: A report that gives only one example offers inadequate support for its claim.
apps.spoken: I think this plan is inadequate; we need more time.
apps.writing: Use inadequate when something falls short of what the situation needs.

cloze.s: With only two life jackets for five riders, the boat's safety equipment was ___.

cloze2.s: The tiny lamp gave ___ light for reading, so Noor carried her book to the window.

misuse.s: The inadequate meal was so huge that no one could finish it.
misuse.why: Inadequate means not enough; a meal too big to finish is more than enough.

words.def: Not steady or matching; changing from one time to another.
words.ex: The team was inconsistent: it won three games and then lost four in a row.
words.ex2: Her story was inconsistent, since she said first that she was home and later that she was at the store.
words.nonExample: A runner who finishes every race in almost the same time is not inconsistent.
words.rel: when something does not fit or work

apps.academic: A scientist rechecks any result that is inconsistent with the prediction.
apps.spoken: Your answers are inconsistent; first you said yes and now you say no.
apps.writing: Use inconsistent for behavior that changes without a reason, or for facts that do not match.

cloze.s: The bakery's bread was ___: Monday's loaf was crisp and golden, but Tuesday's was pale and soft.

cloze2.s: Because the witness's two descriptions of the car did not match, the detective called her account ___.

misuse.s: His inconsistent habits meant he did exactly the same thing at exactly the same time every day.
misuse.why: Inconsistent means not steady; doing the same thing every day is steady.

visual.alt: A roller coaster track that rises and drops.

words.def: Having no connection to the topic or question being discussed.
words.ex: Ravi's long story about his dog was irrelevant to the science question.
words.ex2: A judge will not allow evidence that is irrelevant to the case.
words.nonExample: Using a photograph that shows the exact event you are describing is not irrelevant.

segs.m: connected to the matter at hand

morph.note: The prefix in- is spelled ir- before r.

words.rel: when something does not fit or work

apps.academic: Delete details that are irrelevant to your claim so readers stay focused.
apps.spoken: That's irrelevant; let's get back to the question.
apps.writing: Use irrelevant for details that do not help the point.

cloze.s: When we asked about the broken window, the witness's comments about the weather turned out to be ___.

cloze2.s: Cut any sentence that is ___ to your topic, such as a joke in the middle of a lab report.

misuse.s: The speaker's irrelevant example connected perfectly to the main point and made it much clearer.
misuse.why: Irrelevant means not connected to the point; an example that connects perfectly is relevant.

visual.alt: A pizza slice sitting in the middle of a geometry problem.

words.def: So messy or faint that it cannot be read.
words.ex: The old letter was illegible, because the ink had faded to a pale brown smudge.
words.ex2: My brother's handwriting is illegible when he is in a hurry.
words.nonExample: Neat printing in dark ink is not illegible.

morph.note: The prefix in- is spelled il- before l.

apps.academic: A historian may struggle with a document whose writing has become illegible.
apps.spoken: Sorry, my notes are illegible; I wrote them in the car.
apps.writing: Use illegible when writing cannot be read because it is smudged, faded, or messy.

cloze.s: The ink had run in the rain, leaving the address on the envelope completely ___.

cloze2.s: Grandpa's recipe card was so ___ that we could not tell whether it called for one cup of flour or ten.

misuse.s: The teacher praised the illegible essay because every word was clear and easy to read.
misuse.why: Illegible means cannot be read; an essay with every word clear is legible.

visual.alt: A smudged handwritten note with raindrops on it.

words.def: Not following clear reasoning; not making sense.
words.ex: It is illogical to prepare for a spelling test by reading a chapter of your math book.
words.ex2: His argument was illogical, because the conclusion did not follow from any of his reasons.
words.nonExample: A conclusion that follows step by step from the facts is not illogical.

morph.note: The prefix in- is spelled il- before l.

apps.academic: A scientist rejects an illogical explanation that cannot match the data.
apps.spoken: It's illogical to study after the test is over.
apps.writing: Use illogical for reasoning with a gap, or a conclusion that does not follow.

cloze.s: Because the reasons did not support the conclusion, the debate judge called the argument ___.

cloze2.s: Saving money by buying three of the same expensive gadget is a ___ plan.

misuse.s: Everyone agreed his illogical plan made perfect sense, since each step followed clearly from the last.
misuse.why: Illogical means not following clear reasoning; steps that follow clearly are logical.

visual.alt: A puzzle piece that does not fit, beside a question mark.

words.def: Not fully grown or developed, or acting in a way that is younger than one's age.
words.ex: The immature tomatoes were still small and green, so we left them on the vine.
words.ex2: It was immature of the players to laugh at the losing team instead of shaking hands.
words.nonExample: A calm, thoughtful reply to a hard question is not immature.

morph.note: The prefix in- is spelled im- before m.

apps.academic: Biologists compare the immature and adult forms of an insect.
apps.spoken: Throwing food at lunch is immature.
apps.writing: Use immature for things not yet fully grown, and for childish behavior.

cloze.s: The ___ peaches were hard and green, so they would not be ready to pick for weeks.

cloze2.s: Slamming the door and refusing to talk was an ___ way to handle a disagreement.

misuse.s: The fully grown oak was an immature tree that had only just sprouted this spring.
misuse.why: Immature means not fully grown; a fully grown oak is mature.

visual.alt: Small green tomatoes on a vine beside a seedling.

words.def: Not sensible or useful in real life; hard to carry out.
words.ex: Wearing smooth-soled dress shoes to hike a rocky trail is impractical.
words.ex2: The inventor's giant umbrella was impractical because no doorway was wide enough to carry it through.
words.nonExample: A sturdy backpack with pockets for school supplies is not impractical.

segs.m: sensible and useful in real life

morph.note: The prefix in- is spelled im- before p.

words.rel: when something does not fit or work

apps.academic: Engineers test whether a design is impractical before they build it.
apps.spoken: That's a nice idea, but it's impractical.
apps.writing: Use impractical for ideas that sound good but would not work in real life.

cloze.s: Building a bridge of paper straws to carry heavy trucks is an ___ plan.

cloze2.s: Because glass slippers break so easily, they would be ___ for running to catch a bus.

misuse.s: A raincoat made of paper is impractical, so it is the perfect choice for a downpour.
misuse.why: A paper raincoat would fall apart in the rain; impractical means not useful in real life.

visual.alt: Dress shoes at the foot of a rocky mountain trail.

words.def: Too great to be counted, sized up, or fully described.
words.ex: Her kindness during the move meant an immeasurable amount to our family.
words.ex2: The flood caused immeasurable damage, and crews could not count everything it had destroyed.
words.nonExample: The length of a table, found with a ruler, is not immeasurable.

morph.note: The prefix in- is spelled im- before m.

apps.academic: Historians say some losses of war are immeasurable, even when numbers are counted.
apps.spoken: The help you gave us is immeasurable.
apps.writing: Use immeasurable for feelings, losses, or sizes too great for numbers.

cloze.s: Because no tool could capture how much joy the puppy brought, the family said its value was ___.

cloze2.s: The new library gave the town ___ benefits that no list of numbers could fully capture.

misuse.s: The length of the desk was immeasurable, so we easily found it with a ruler.
misuse.why: Immeasurable means too great to measure; a desk length found with a ruler is measurable.

visual.alt: A short ruler beside a sky full of stars, too large to measure.

words.def: Too special or rare to be swapped for something else.
words.ex: The torn photograph of her grandparents was irreplaceable to Salma.
words.ex2: Because only one copy of the old map existed, the museum treated it as irreplaceable.
words.nonExample: A pencil from a box of twenty-four is not irreplaceable.

segs.m: able to be swapped for another

morph.note: The prefix in- is spelled ir- before r.

apps.academic: Archaeologists protect irreplaceable objects because once they are damaged, they cannot be remade.
apps.spoken: My sketchbook is irreplaceable; it has every drawing I have made this year.
apps.writing: Use irreplaceable for people, objects, or memories that nothing else can stand in for.

cloze.s: Grandpa's handmade violin was ___; no store could sell another one just like it.

cloze2.s: Losing the only copy of the class's oral history project meant losing something ___.

misuse.s: The pencil was so irreplaceable that she bought a new one for pennies that afternoon.
misuse.why: Irreplaceable means nothing else can take its place; a cheap pencil is easy to replace.

visual.alt: An old violin beside a framed family photo.

words.def: Not taking proper care of duties, or acting without thinking how others will be affected.
words.ex: It was irresponsible to leave the campfire burning when we went to sleep.
words.ex2: The irresponsible pet owner forgot to feed the cat for two days.
words.nonExample: Returning a borrowed book on time is not irresponsible.

segs.m: able to be trusted with a duty

morph.note: The prefix in- is spelled ir- before r.

apps.academic: Historians judge whether leaders made irresponsible decisions that put their citizens at risk.
apps.spoken: Leaving your bike unlocked is irresponsible.
apps.writing: Use irresponsible when a character ignores a duty and others are affected.

cloze.s: It was ___ of Theo to forget the keys, because the whole team had to wait outside in the rain.

cloze2.s: Texting while riding a bike down a busy street is ___ and could hurt someone.

misuse.s: The irresponsible lifeguard watched the swimmers carefully and never looked away.
misuse.why: Irresponsible means ignoring a duty; watching carefully is doing the duty.

visual.alt: A campfire left burning beside a warning sign.

passage.title: The Box in the Basement
paras: Every Saturday, Zeynep helped at the town's historical society, where a donated box of papers had just arrived. The basement room was dim, and the single lamp was inadequate for reading old writing, so she carried a flashlight from table to table.

The first letters she opened were nearly illegible. Water had once soaked the box, and the ink had faded into brown clouds. Her partner, Marcus, groaned and flicked a page across the table. Ms. Adeyemi, the archivist, raised an eyebrow. "Tossing old paper around is immature," she said calmly. "These letters are irreplaceable. If one tears, nobody can make another."

Marcus apologized and went back to work. Soon he spotted a problem. "The labels are inconsistent," he said. "This folder says 1952, but a letter inside mentions an event from 1961." Zeynep frowned. "That is illogical. A folder from 1952 cannot hold a letter about something that happened later." Ms. Adeyemi nodded. "Good thinking. Someone mixed up the dates, so we will have to check every page."

A few items were irrelevant to the project. A folded grocery list and three bus tickets had nothing to do with the history of the town, so Zeynep set them aside in a separate envelope. Marcus suggested scanning everything into the computer at once, but Ms. Adeyemi shook her head. "We have one old scanner, so that plan is impractical. We will start with the most fragile pages."

By closing time they had saved twelve letters. One of them described how neighbors had built the town's first library, and its last line called the library's value to the community immeasurable. "Leaving these in a damp box another winter would have been irresponsible," Ms. Adeyemi said. Zeynep smiled. The basement lamp was not much, she thought, but the work done under it had been worth far more.

qs.q: In paragraph 2, the word "irreplaceable" most nearly means
choices: very expensive to buy
easy to fix with tape
too special to be swapped for something else
old and covered with dust
qs.why: Ms. Adeyemi explains that if one letter tears, nobody can make another, so each one cannot be replaced.

qs.q: Why does Ms. Adeyemi call Marcus's behavior immature?
choices: He treated fragile papers in a careless, childish way.
He is younger than the other volunteers.
He did not know how to read old handwriting.
He asked too many questions about the labels.
qs.why: Marcus flicked a page across the table, which treats a fragile letter like a toy; that is childish, not a matter of his age or skill.

qs.q: Which detail best shows that the folder labels were inconsistent?
choices: The basement was dim and the lamp was small.
A folder marked 1952 held a letter about an event from 1961.
A grocery list and three bus tickets were in the box.
The ink on the first letters had faded into brown clouds.
qs.why: A label and the paper inside disagree about the date, which is what inconsistent means.

qs.q: Why does Ms. Adeyemi say that scanning everything at once is impractical?
choices: Scanning would damage every letter.
The computer does not work in the basement.
Marcus does not know how to use a scanner.
The society has only one old scanner, so the plan will not work well.
qs.why: She says they have one old scanner and chooses a smaller plan, so the big plan is not workable in real life.

qs.q: Which statement best expresses a central idea of the passage?
choices: Basements are bad places to store paper.
Careful work can save pieces of the past that cannot be replaced.
Letters from the past are less important than computers.
Volunteers should never disagree with an archivist.
qs.why: The group saves fragile letters carefully, and the final line stresses that this work was worth far more than the lamp's small light.

teacher.overview: Students learn ten adjectives made with the negating prefix in- and its spelling changes il-, im-, and ir-, use the base word to predict meaning and spelling, read a short archive story, and practice using the words to judge plans, writing, arguments, and behavior.

notes.va.inadequate.adj: Start with the base: adequate means enough. Put adequate and inadequate on a line and ask students to find real examples of each. Inadequate is not the same as terrible; something can almost be enough and still be inadequate.
notes.va.inconsistent.adj: Two related meanings: not steady over time (a team) and not matching (two stories). Both come from the base idea of holding together. Ask which meaning each example uses.
notes.va.irrelevant.adj: The double r is the lesson: ir- plus relevant. Use it as a writing tool: students cross out irrelevant sentences in a paragraph. Irrelevant is about connection to a topic, not about whether something is interesting.
notes.va.illegible.adj: Illegible is about reading, not about meaning: a clearly printed sentence can still be confusing, but it is legible. Contrast with illogical, which is about reasoning. Both begin with il- before a base starting with l.
notes.va.illogical.adj: Illogical is not the same as wrong. An argument can have true statements and still be illogical if the steps do not connect. Ask students to find the missing step in a faulty argument.
notes.va.immature.adj: Two senses, physical and behavioral, share one idea: not yet developed. When describing people, immature can sound harsh; discuss how to say it about behavior rather than about a person. The im- spelling comes before m.
notes.va.impractical.adj: Impractical is not the same as impossible. An impractical plan could be done but would not work well. Pair with immeasurable to show im- before p and m.
notes.va.immeasurable.adj: Immeasurable is often used for feelings and effects, where it means 'too great to put a number on'. Students may think it means 'tiny'; clear that up with the base measurable. The double m is a fingerprint of the im- prefix.
notes.va.irreplaceable.adj: Irreplaceable is about uniqueness, not price: a handwritten letter can be irreplaceable and cost nothing. Ask for one irreplaceable thing in the classroom and one that is easy to replace.
notes.va.irresponsible.adj: Irresponsible includes the effect on others: a person can take a risk with their own homework without being irresponsible toward a team. Link back to impulsive and cautious from unit 1.

teacher.model: Think-aloud: 'I see illegible. The base is legible, which means able to be read. The base starts with l, so in- becomes il-. Il plus legible gives illegible: not able to be read. In the story, the ink faded, so the letters cannot be read. The word fits.'

Which of these ten words could describe a person, and which could describe only things?
misconceptions: Every word that starts with in- means 'not' (inject and inside do not).
The prefixes il-, im-, and ir- are three unrelated prefixes.
Illogical means the same as wrong.
extend: Make a chart of 15 base words and decide which spelling of the prefix each needs, then check with a dictionary.
Write a short paragraph describing a plan using inadequate, impractical, and irrelevant correctly.
teacher.reviewAdvice: Revisit impulsive from unit 1 and subtle and evident from unit 2 in a two-day quick check; ask which of those would pair naturally with irresponsible, inconsistent, or illogical. Return to the prefix rule at one week with five new words (for example impossible, irregular, illegal).

frames: The ___ is inadequate because there is not enough ___.
The base word is ___, so the prefix is spelled ___ because it begins with the letter ___.

wida.oral: Partner A says a base word (for example, relevant). Partner B adds the correct prefix, says the new word, gives its meaning, and uses it in a sentence.

needsReview: Spanish glosses not reviewed by a native speaker: insuficiente (inadequate; 'inadecuado' also exists but means unsuitable), poco práctico, inconmensurable, irreemplazable, inmaduro.

Morphology: the assimilation rule (in- spelled il- before l, im- before b/m/p, ir- before r) is standard; no etymological claims are made beyond the meaning 'not'. Confirm the in- 'not' part is separated clearly from in- meaning 'in or into'.
Sense boundary: immature and inconsistent each carry two close senses folded into one definition; confirm the wording is clear for grade 6.
Fact claims in word records: archaeologists protect irreplaceable objects; engineers test designs; historians judge decisions. General statements believed accurate.
Passage is fiction; no factual claims.
